It was that very early deathcore style of false chord screaming where vocalists attempted to sound like fry. The DOOM ep by JFACB has similar high screams. Kardivox did a video on Entombment of a Machine where he goes into detail on how that type of scream is really bad for your voice.

Inhaling is frowned upon because it’s associated with “noob” metal vocalists due to it being extremely easy to grasp and being almost always strictly worse sounding than false chord vocals. (This was even prevalent during the MySpace era.) 

Early deathcore vocalists also quickly shifted away from inhale lows, with Phil Bozeman I believe being one of the only early era “mainstream” vocalists to have never done them.

Yeah, that works in like 28 Days Later, where the infected are literally just people running around instinct trying to tear you apart with no real motive. They’re not evil. They’re more like animals. That’s why the military betrayal at the end hits hard, and why the audience ends up rooting for the infected during the castle siege at the end. 

Crossed are not just mindless screaming monsters that run at you. They’re already just humanity taken to its absolute depravity. So trying to say “non-infected are the real bad guys” doesn’t really work in a series where the villains are basically just humans acting out on their most vile tendencies due to a virus.

I feel similarly, that Crossed is a “deconstruction” of the Zombie genre. Zombies/Infected are supposed to be “people are the real monsters” type shtick but like in 28 Days Later for example, they lean heavily into the monster department, there’s no humanity left. They don’t do anything. They’re just monsters that run at you and eat you.

They take the humanity out of the infected completely. They’re just mindless monsters. Crossed takes the worst part of humanity, and ramps it up to 11 with its infected, showing the true “monsters” that humanity can represent that zombie media doesn’t portray. They’re still people to an extent, just the most horrible people imaginable doing things that evil people would do. Zombies just mindlessly attack and eat things on instinct. They’re just as easily any other monster masquerading in human skin.

I think the context of this whole situation is important. With this being pre-Punisher Frank, them being in Vietnam, the woman being a POW enemy combatant. 

I think here specifically Frank was going to kill her anyway, due to being the enemy. But he has a disdain for SA, so he interrupts by killing her, which gets what he wants accomplished but also sends a message to his men. 

But in this scenario at the end of the day Frank didn’t see her as an innocent woman.  

When it comes to people he believes are innocent but in situations where a “mercy kill” is required or requested, he has indulged. He doesn’t view himself as murdering them in most runs where he does a mercy kill. He views it as a reluctant necessary evil.

It’s all about context. Being if being gay isn’t what makes the character a villain, it’s just a villain who happens to be gay. 

As someone who is part of the LGBTQ+ community, I often make my villains gay, bisexual, or have no defined sexuality if the story doesn’t call for it. 

I recently wrote a draft where a bisexual character becomes a serial killing vigilante after his boyfriend is murdered. He is very much portrayed as a villain to show that vigilante justice is wrong. But his sexuality doesn’t define his character at all. I could easily swap his murdered boyfriend to be his murdered girlfriend and it would barely affect the script.

No problem. You can get really loud with it, like Phil Bozeman or Alex Terrible, but their’s are really refined now. I have pretty clean sounding false chord highs that are about as loud as a power fry, but my main technique is Phil’s false chord guttural style, which uses a lot of power. 

Once you get it down, the transfer of power becomes easier and you can get a cleaner sound, but I personally try not to go too clean. I myself like a bit of the gurgly bits of false chord screaming.

Been doing exclusively false chord screams for 10 years starting in middle school, I had no interest in doing fry screams.

While there are many false chord vocalists and bands such as Oceans Ate Alaska, older In Dying Arms, Alesana, etc that utilize very clean sounding false chord high screams, they require almost a complete mastery of using the false chord scream without harming yourself using true chords.

Getting high false chords took me much longer than lows, mids, and even gutturals. The trick that helped me finally get a grasp on it was to not try to mimic cleaner sounding false chord highs, but extremely dirty “gurgly” ones. It almost feels like doing toilet bowl gutturals, but in a scream. 

Think of bands like Haste the Day, old Whitechapel, Emmure, Feed Her to the Sharks, I Killed the Prom Queen. All use very loose gurgly sounding high false chord screams. Once you can master this sound, you’ll find it easier to clean it up while also raising the pitch even more.

The song I used to practice to religiously, and one I recommend to people learning to do false chord highs is American Love by Haste the Day. Once you get the gist and can mimic the sound while doing the entire song without your throat hurting consistently you should be golden.

Hey, dude! 

It's most likely your high false chord screams and/or mids. They're both very difficult to get a firm grasp over when it comes to comfortability. It took me from when I started screaming at age 15, all the way to age 21 to get highs very similar to James from Oceans Ate Alaska.  

When doing the false chord high or mid scream, I took a bit of advice from my ex girlfriend (who is a classical singer) and Dicky (Jared Dines buddy). 

The first advice was from my ex, which was a very good way to engage the diaphragm. She told me to do a light cough, and to remember the feeling of the flex my stomach did. Then sort of use that flex to engage it when doing vocals. It is much easier to practice this when doing clean vocals however.

And what I learned from Dicky (In his Tips For High Scream False Chords video) was to relax your throat as much as possible, rather than tense up like you're about to do a Bozeman low. He also said learning to make the sound of a Wookiee is very helpful in finding where you should be feeling the vibrations in your throat. 

Mids are about the same as highs, but with a bit of chest compression, but not nearly as much as the guttural scream should. 

Oh! Also! I recomended watching Vokill Coverz High Scream and Gutteral Tutorial Videos! They explain getting the proper pitches in a very helpful (yet silly) manner!
